description: Promises, async/await and the event loop.

questions.question: What are the three states of a Promise?
What is the purpose of then, catch, and finally on a promise?
questions.answer:
then handles the fulfilled value, catch handles the rejection, and finally runs cleanup regardless of the outcome while passing the result through.

code:
const result = await fetch(url)
  .then(res => res.json())
  .catch(err => { throw new Error('fetch failed: ' + err); })
  .finally(() => cleanup());

real example:
Making test setup that always closes a resource uses finally so failures still run post-test cleanup.

questions.question: Why is Promise.all useful and what happens on rejection?
questions.answer:
Promise.all resolves with an array of values when every promise fulfills, and rejects as soon as any single promise rejects, discarding the rest.

code:
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetch('/a'), fetch('/b')]);

real example:
Loading two independent checkout endpoints in parallel cuts test time, and the earliest failure stops the suite early.

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.allSettled and Promise.all?
What does Promise.race do?
questions.answer:
Promise.race settles as soon as the first promise settles, returning its value or reason while ignoring every other promise's outcome.

code:
const winner = await Promise.race([
  request(),
  timeout(5000),
]);

real example:
Capping a slow request with a timeout promise via race gives a quick failure instead of an endless client hang.

questions.question: What is async/await and how does it improve on promise chains?
What happens when you await a non-promise value?
questions.answer:
await always returns the value directly for non-promises, wrapping it into an already-resolved promise internally. It adds no delay for plain values.

code:
const x = await 42;
console.log(x);  // 42

real example:
Helpers that sometimes return a promise and sometimes a plain value stay usable with await either way, which simplifies fixture functions.

questions.question: How do you catch errors thrown inside an async function?
What is the event loop in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
The event loop is the mechanism that processes the call stack and the message queue, running JavaScript's single thread while letting async callbacks execute in order.

code:
console.log('start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
console.log('end');  // start, end, timeout

real example:
Knowing that timers run after the current script explains why an immediate check after page.click still needs an await.

questions.question: What is the difference between a microtask and a macrotask?
questions.answer:
Microtasks such as promise callbacks run before the next macrotask such as setTimeout or an event handler. Between macrotasks the microtask queue is fully drained.

code:
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('micro'));
setTimeout(() => console.log('macro'), 0);
console.log('sync');  // sync, micro, macro

real example:
The ordering sync, then promise, then timer explains surprising log sequences and flaky timeout assumptions in tests.

questions.question: Why do promises run before setTimeout callbacks?
questions.answer:
Promise reactions are microtasks drained until empty right after the current synchronous code, while setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks scheduled for later task turns.

code:
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(1));
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);  // 1 then 2

real example:
Waiting for a promise result before polling a timeout interval only holds for the microtask drain, not the entire task.

questions.question: What is callback-based toPromise conversion and how is it done?
What does awaiting inside a loop do differently from Promise.all?
questions.answer:
Awaited sequentially, each iteration waits for the previous promise, running one by one. Promise.all runs all promises concurrently and waits for all to finish.

code:
for (const url of urls) await fetch(url);      // sequential
await Promise.all(urls.map(u => fetch(u)));    // parallel

real example:
Creating one-by-one test records stays sequential to respect API rate limits, while read-only checks parallelize.

questions.question: How do you convert an array of promises into their values cleanly?
What is the best practice for handling unhandled promise rejections?
Why do you need await for waits in Playwright rather than fixed sleep?
questions.answer:
Playwright auto-waits for the actionability of elements with built-in retries, so awaiting locator methods handles slow renders without arbitrary sleeps.

code:
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

real example:
Replacing page.waitForTimeout(3000) with expect(locator).toBeVisible() removes flaky fixed sleeps and speeds the whole suite.
